faq.a: Yes, if the inciting cause (e.g., uncontrolled hypertension) is removed early, regression of wall thickness can occur.
faq.q: Can cardiac hypertrophy be completely reversed?

faq.a: ACE‑Is directly reduce afterload and inhibit fibrosis, whereas β‑blockers mainly control rate and may worsen asthma.
faq.q: Why is an ACE‑I preferred over a β‑blocker in most cases?

faq.a: A sustained, forceful apex beat with a narrow pulse pressure suggests concentric; a displaced, hyperdynamic apex with a wide pulse pressure suggests eccentric.
faq.q: What sign distinguishes concentric from eccentric hypertrophy on exam?

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with uncontrolled hypertension presents with dyspnoea. Which investigation best confirms the type of hypertrophy and why? — Echocardiography; it measures wall thickness and chamber dimensions.

You find a tall R wave in V6 on ECG but no symptoms. How do you decide if treatment is needed? — Correlate with blood pressure and echo; isolated ECG changes without hypertrophy do not require therapy.
A patient with rheumatic mitral regurgitation develops LV dilation. What is the primary management goal? — Reduce preload with diuretics and consider surgical repair when feasible.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a child with severe anaemia shows a hyperdynamic apex. How does anaemia cause eccentric hypertrophy? — Chronic volume overload from high cardiac output leads to chamber dilation.
What is the first emergency step for a patient with acute pulmonary oedema due to hypertensive crisis? — Give IV loop diuretic and supplemental oxygen while arranging rapid BP control.
Why would you avoid high‑dose non‑selective β‑blockers in a patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and asthma? — They can precipitate bronchospasm and worsen outflow obstruction.
How does chronic HIV infection contribute to cardiac hypertrophy? — HIV‑associated hypertension and chronic inflammation promote pressure overload and fibrosis.

A young athlete has an LV wall thickness of 12 mm on echo. How do you differentiate physiological from pathological hypertrophy? — Assess training history, blood pressure, symptoms, and lack of fibrosis; physiological hypertrophy is symmetric, without diastolic dysfunction.
ai.title: Cardiac Hypertrophy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Cardiac hypertrophy is the heart's adaptive thickening of muscle in response to pressure or volume overload. Distinguish physiological from pathological forms, identify common causes in low‑resource settings, and know the key investigations and management steps.

b: Concentric → pressure (e.g., hypertension, aortic stenosis)
Eccentric → volume (e.g., regurgitant lesions, anemia)
Physiological (athlete) vs pathological
sections.p: Hypertrophy is an increase in myocardial mass. It can be concentric (wall thickening) from pressure overload or eccentric (chamber dilation) from volume overload. In low‑resource hospitals, common triggers include hypertension, rheumatic heart disease, anemia from malaria or sickle cell, and chronic HIV infection.

b: Fibrosis → stiff ventricle → diastolic dysfunction
Neuro‑hormonal activation (RAAS, sympathetic) worsens remodeling
Reversible if cause removed early
sections.p: Pathological hypertrophy follows the law of Laplace: increased wall stress leads to myocyte enlargement and fibrosis, eventually impairing diastolic filling and precipitating heart failure.

b: Hypertension → sustained BP >140/90 mmHg
Aortic stenosis → crescendo‑decrescendo systolic murmur, radiates to carotids
Regurgitant lesions → holosystolic murmur, displaced PMI
sections.p: Patients may present with dyspnoea, fatigue, or chest pain. In low‑resource settings, look for signs of pressure overload (systolic murmur, displaced apex) or volume overload (wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses).

t.b: Does the ECG show voltage criteria for LVH? → Tall R waves in V5‑V6, deep S in V1 suggest hypertrophy; may be normal in early disease.
Is there cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion? → Enlarged cardiac silhouette supports chronic overload; absent in early stages.
What is wall thickness and chamber size? → Concentric: IVS/LV posterior wall ≥12 mm; Eccentric: LV end‑diastolic dimension >55 mm. If echo unavailable, rely on clinical signs and ECG.
Is hypertension present? → BP ≥140/90 mmHg confirms pressure overload; treat aggressively.
Is anemia contributing to volume overload? → Hb <10 g/dL suggests anemia from malaria, sickle cell, or chronic disease.

b: Control hypertension: ACE‑I or ARB (reduce afterload, limit fibrosis)
Aortic stenosis: refer for valve replacement when feasible; in low‑resource settings, consider balloon valvuloplasty if surgery unavailable
Regurgitant lesions: diuretics for volume control, consider surgery if severe
Treat anemia: iron, antimalarials, sickle‑cell management
Avoid: non‑selective β‑blockers in severe asthma, high‑dose diuretics without monitoring electrolytes
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then use drugs that reduce afterload or preload and block maladaptive remodeling.

b: Ask about blood pressure control and symptoms of valve disease
Palpate a displaced, sustained apex beat in concentric hypertrophy
Listen for murmurs: systolic ejection murmur (stenosis) vs holosystolic murmur (regurgitation)
If acute decompensation: give IV furosemide and oxygen, then address underlying cause
sections.p: Focus on differentiating pressure vs volume overload, recognizing reversible causes, and knowing the first emergency step.

b: Assuming tall ECG voltages always mean pathology
Missing rheumatic valve disease in young adults
Delaying antihypertensive therapy because symptoms are mild
sections.p: Mistaking physiological athlete’s heart for disease, ignoring anemia as a volume overload driver, and over‑relying on ECG when echo is unavailable.
